title: MOS Device Models
intro: Amplifier analysis replaces the transistor with a linear small-signal model around the bias point.

blocks.text: For small signals around a bias point the transistor in saturation is a voltage-controlled current source plus a resistor and capacitors:

blocks.source:
id = gm*vgs + gmb*vbs + vds/ro

gm  = 2*ID/Vov
gmb = eta*gm       (eta about 0.1 - 0.3)
ro  = 1/(lambda*ID)

blocks.text: A useful figure of merit is the intrinsic gain gm*ro = 2/(lambda*Vov). It is the maximum voltage gain a single transistor can provide, and it drops with scaling because lambda grows as L shrinks.

items: Gate-source Cgs: about (2/3)*W*L*Cox plus overlap in saturation.
Gate-drain Cgd: mostly overlap capacitance W*Cov in saturation. Small but important because of the Miller effect.
Source/drain-bulk Csb, Cdb: reverse-biased junction capacitances that fall with reverse voltage.
The transit frequency fT = gm / (2*pi*(Cgs + Cgd)) is the frequency at which the current gain falls to one.

blocks.text: Hole mobility is about 2 to 4 times lower than electron mobility, so a PMOS needs 2 to 4 times the W/L for the same gm and has lower fT. Short-channel devices of both types have comparable speeds because velocity saturation reduces the difference.

To reduce drain/source junction capacitance, wide transistors are split into several parallel fingers that share diffusion regions. The same finger structure reduces gate resistance, which would otherwise add thermal noise and slow the gate.

blocks.title: Intrinsic gain
blocks.text: A transistor has Vov = 0.2 V and lambda = 0.2 V^-1 at its operating length. Find gm*ro. What if the length is doubled?
solution: Doubling L halves lambda, so gm*ro = 100. Intrinsic gain therefore rises with L but speed falls.
blocks.answer: gm*ro = 50, rising to 100 when L doubles.

blocks.title: Transit frequency
blocks.text: gm = 2 mS, Cgs = 20 fF, Cgd = 5 fF. Estimate fT.
